title: How Much Room Does the Situation Leave?
scopeNote: This keeps the live strength control and the two contrasting settings. Both are needed: one setting shows compression, and only a second shows that the ordering itself depends on what is afforded. The ranking prediction, the additional settings, the explicit aggregation demonstration and the transfer exercise stay in the longer version.
summary: Four fictional people observed in two settings, with one slider for how much the setting dictates behaviour. Raising it squeezes the people together without changing them, and the two settings never agree about who does most.
learningObjectives: Explain what a strong situation does to observed between-person variation.
Explain why low observed behavioural variance is not evidence of low trait variance.
Distinguish situational constraint from situational affordance.
Explain why two settings that both leave room can still rank the same people differently.
Say why neither personality mattering more nor situations mattering more is a defensible summary.
interactionTypes: a single live control over how much the settings dictate
a slopegraph joining each person across the two settings
live spread figures for each setting
a live check of whether the two settings agree about the ordering
a guided setting showing near-total compression
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Nothing is asked about the learner.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with the strength a native range input carrying a live value output. Each person's line is labelled with their name and value at both ends, so no line has to be traced across the figure or told apart by colour. The chart carries a description giving every person's value in both settings, both spreads, and whether the two settings agree about the ordering, so the crossing pattern is available as text. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: Four invented people and two invented settings, with behaviour generated from a formula rather than observed. The numbers are units of nothing in particular and nothing here describes or predicts any real person.
simulationNotes: Behaviour is the setting's demand weighted by strength plus the person's trait, amplified by a gain of 1.35 about the scale midpoint, weighted by one minus strength. The trait used is the one that setting affords, which is what makes the two settings rank people differently: the cast is arranged so the party ranks by sociability and the handover by conscientiousness, and the two orderings are reversed at the extremes. At full strength everyone converges on the demand, so the spread falls from about 26 to about 1 without any person changing. The ordering remains technically different even then, and the readout says so explicitly rather than reporting a difference that is within a point or two as though it still mattered.
readmeTopic: why the same people look alike in one setting and quite different in another
